claims.text: The target material is a quaternary equiatomic, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy is a chemically disordered FCC solid solution with high configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion.
The target alloy is mechanistically similar to CoCrFeMnNi or CoCrFeNi alloys.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate below approximately 100 K.
Cryogenic strain-rate insensitivity results from a transition away from thermally activated dislocation glide toward deformation dominated by nanotwinning and stacking-fault formation.
Nanotwins and stacking faults form during cryogenic deformation and contribute to the strength, ductility, and work hardening of Cantor-type alloys.
Nanotwins and stacking faults act as barriers to dislocation motion.
At room temperature, yield strength is strongly strain-rate dependent.
Room- or higher-temperature deformation is rate-controlled by thermally activated dislocations overcoming nanoscale clusters or short-range order.
At low temperature, the activation energy for dislocation glide over short-range-order clusters becomes negligible relative to thermal energy.
Slip and deformation twinning can operate together in FCC CoCrFeMnNi over approximately 25–600 °C.
Dislocation glide provides a plausible dislocation-based deformation mechanism in Cantor-type FCC alloys.
The yield-strength-versus-strain-rate curve will have a steep positive slope at room temperature and an approximately zero slope at cryogenic temperature.
Conventional FCC alloys generally weaken with increasing temperature and strengthen with increasing strain rate through thermally activated dislocation motion.
The proposed mechanism may fail if deformation induces an FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC phase transformation.
The proposed mechanism may fail when precipitates dominate strengthening.
The transition temperature depends on the stacking-fault energy and short-range-order binding energy of the particular quaternary alloy.
Oxygen or other interstitials could alter the deformation mechanism.

A cryogenic strain-rate sensitivity exponent greater than 0.05, or observation of exclusively thermally activated dislocation glide without dominant twins or stacking faults, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes cryogenic rate insensitivity to a transition to an athermal twinning/stacking-fault mechanism, while the mechanism field alternatively attributes it to the activation energy for glide becoming negligible relative to thermal energy. These are distinct explanations, and the latter is internally problematic at lower temperature where thermal energy decreases.

The initial state is specified as single-phase FCC, but the boundary acknowledges that closely related alloys may contain or develop HCP material under pressure or cryogenic deformation. The hypothesis does not establish that the unspecified quaternary target remains single-phase FCC during testing.
